section_summary: This section brings together occupation-era materials on Japan’s postwar constitutional and governmental transformation, including the English text of the 1946 Constitution, the replacement of “Imperial Japanese Government” with “Japanese Government,” and records concerning Tanzan Ishibashi, the House of Councillors, and Hitoshi Ashida’s proposed cabinet. A substantial group of 1948 documents describes SCAP’s campaign to promote representative local government, citizen participation, decentralization, and the powers of elected prefectural governors under the Local Autonomy Law. The section also records Ashida’s centrist, anti-communist, reconstruction-oriented policy program and the occupation authorities’ efforts to replace centralized and coercive prewar institutions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 776: English Text of “Constitution of Japan”
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards six copies of the English text of the Constitution of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 776 encloses six copies of the final English text of the 'Constitution of Japan', after the Diet's changes sent in Despatch No. 713.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1061: Designation of Japanese Government in Official Correspondence
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP’s decision to use “Japanese Government” instead of “Imperial Japanese Government” in official documents.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1061: SCAP correspondence will now say 'Japanese Government', an internal practice prompted by the new Constitution's avoidance of 'Imperial'.

subfiles.title: Staff Memorandum No. 43: Designation of Japanese Government
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers and Far East Command
subfiles.to: SCAP and Far East Command personnel
subfiles.about: Orders the use of “Japanese Government” in headquarters correspondence and documents.
subfiles.summary: Staff Memorandum No. 43 directs that Japan's national government be called the 'Japanese Government', not the 'Imperial Japanese Government', in headquarters documents.

subfiles.title: The Constitution of Japan
subfiles.about: Provides the official English text of Japan’s postwar Constitution as promulgated on November 3, 1946.
subfiles.summary: The document contains Hirohito’s promulgation, the countersignatures of the Yoshida cabinet, the preamble, and all eleven chapters and 103 articles. It establishes popular sovereignty, a symbolic emperor, renunciation of war, fundamental rights, a bicameral Diet, cabinet government, judicial independence, public financial control, and local autonomy. Its supplementary provisions prescribe implementation six months after promulgation and transitional arrangements for officials and the House of Councillors.

subfiles.title: Record Copy Replacement Sheet for Despatch No. 1208
subfiles.about: Marks the attached copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 1208 as the record copy replacing an unreturned original action copy.
subfiles.summary: Form designating the attached copy of Despatch No. 1208 the record copy because the original was not returned to Central Records.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1208: Status Under SCAPIN 550 of Tanzan Ishibashi
subfiles.about: Forwards a Government Section memorandum recommending Tanzan Ishibashi’s removal from public office.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1208 sends a memorandum on Tanzan Ishibashi recommending his removal and exclusion from government under SCAPIN 550, Category G.

subfiles.title: Record Copy Replacement Sheet for Tokyo Despatch
subfiles.about: Designates the attached Tokyo despatch as a replacement record copy for an unreturned original.
subfiles.summary: Form noting the original action copy of a Tokyo despatch was not returned; the replacement is to be filed with DC/R.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1390: Rules Established by the House of Councillors
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards an English translation of the procedural rules adopted by Japan’s House of Councillors.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1390 encloses a Government Section pamphlet translating the House of Councillors' rules adopted in 1947.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 118: Policy of New Ashida Government
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Hitoshi Ashida’s account of the policies and political basis of his prospective coalition cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ashida tells Sebald he has MacArthur's and Whitney's support and left Socialist backing, and promises international trust, democratization, economic reconstruction, moderate labor support and firm action against extremists.

subfiles.title: Statement Read by Dr. Hitoshi Ashida to General MacArthur
subfiles.about: Outlines the proposed Ashida cabinet’s centrist political, social, and economic program.
subfiles.summary: Ashida's statement to MacArthur: a 'middle of the road' government, Potsdam compliance, political purification, anti-inflation production, key industry priority and action against communist labor influence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 269: Prefectural Conferences on the Local Autonomy Law
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP-sponsored prefectural conferences and summarizes five instructional papers on democratic local government.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 269: Local Government Division two-day prefectural conferences on local autonomy, covering elections, recall, assemblies, finance and public information; begun in Sendai and Ibaraki.

subfiles.title: Local Government Division Paper No. 1: Representative Government
subfiles.from: Cecil G. Tilton, SCAP Local Government Division
subfiles.about: Explains representative government and urges Japanese citizens to exercise their new rights and responsibilities under the Constitution and Local Autonomy Law.
subfiles.summary: Tilton contrasts democratic government with the centralized Meiji system created by Itō and Yamagata and argues that strong local institutions are essential checks on national power. He explains citizen powers of recall, initiative, investigation, and legal action, while condemning the abolished Tonari Gumi and related compulsory neighborhood organizations as mechanisms of wartime regimentation. The address urges women’s participation, responsible taxation, civic pride, political parties, and active public oversight, presenting American prosperity and reconstruction aid as products of democratic freedom.

subfiles.title: Local Government Division Paper No. 2: Powers and Responsibilities of the Office of Governor
subfiles.from: Michael E. Nolan, SCAP Local Government Division
subfiles.about: Describes how the Local Autonomy Law transformed the Japanese prefectural governor from a central-government agent into a democratically constrained local executive.
subfiles.summary: The paper reviews the extensive political, personnel, financial, and supervisory authority exercised by governors under the Meiji-era centralized system and the Home Minister. It then explains the governor’s qualifications, term, ethical restrictions, administrative responsibilities, control of finances and personnel, relations with public-safety and fire-defense bodies, and reliance on assistant governors. It emphasizes cooperation with elected assemblies and explains reconsideration, judicial review, no-confidence votes, dissolution, resignation, and elections as democratic methods for resolving disputes. The document continues beyond page 207, breaking off during its discussion of the governor’s reduced supervisory authority over municipalities.
